sent.t: 34 years I sat beside dying people in this city.
And I can count on one hand the times I watched one of them sit up and ask for breakfast.
11 days before my mother died, she asked me for a cup of coffee and a piece of pan dulce.
I was so happy, honey.
I ran to that kitchen.
I was happy and I was wrong.
My name is Rosa Navarro.
I never carried a stethoscope.
I'm a chaplain.
For 34 years I was a hospice chaplain for Alamo Home Hospice here in San Antonio from 1991 until I retired in 2025 I sat with
close to 3,000 families I was in the kitchen when the phone call came I was in the hallway when the brothers started fighting I was
in the chair at 2 in the morning when nobody else in that house was awake and I saw this one thing over and over again,
the rally The rally is when your dying parent suddenly gets better, for a day, sometimes an afternoon, sometimes two days.
They sit up, they eat, they talk like themselves, they remember your name, your children's names, the dog that died in 2009, they ask for a
specific food from a specific place or they want to call somebody they haven't called in a year, and the whole house starts telephoning the family.
Come quick, that's better.
And that is not better, honey.
Dad is saying goodbye.
Now, I never went to medical school and I'm not going to give you one piece of medical advice in this whole video.
Anything about medicine, anything about symptoms, anything about what to give or not give.
You call your hospice team tonight, not me.
What I can give you is what I saw from that chair beside the bed, 3,000 times, and what the families who did it well did
differently.
Because there is a way to get this right.
It is not complicated.
It is just very easy to get wrong, because everything inside your body is screaming the opposite.
Let me tell you about Walt.
Walt Pruitt was a rancher from Bandera, and I met him in the spring of 1998, 79 years old, a big man with hands like a
catcher's mitt, and he had been in that bed for 11 days barely eating, barely talking, sleeping most of the afternoon.
His wife, Lorraine, had already made the phone calls you make.
The daughter in Houston had come in twice.
The son from Kerrville was there with his wife.
Everybody had said what they came to say.
That is the stage, honey, when the house goes quiet.
And then on a Tuesday morning, Walt sat up and asked for huevos rancheros, not eggs, huevos rancheros with the salsa his wife made and a
flour tortilla and coffee.
And then he asked for the telephone and he called his daughter in Houston and he talked to her for 20 minutes, 20 minutes.
He asked about her garden.
He asked about the grandbaby's tea.
Lorraine called me at nine o'clock at night and she was crying in the good way she said Rosa he ate he ate everything on the
plate he's back he's back Rosa and I said the hardest sentence I ever say to a family I said Lorraine that is beautiful and I'm
so glad you had today and I want you to call your daughter back tomorrow night and tell her again how much you love her because
Walt is not coming back, honey.
Walt is leaving.
Walt died the following Friday, six days after the Huevos Rancheros.
Now here is why I'm telling you this before anything else.
Not one person in that family did anything wrong that Tuesday.
They got a gift and they used it.
Lorraine cooked.
The daughter in Houston laughed on the phone.
The son from Kerrville sat with his daddy in the backyard shade and they talked about a horse they bought love.
That family used the rally.
Most families don't.
Most families spend it on the phone with the insurance company.
So let me give you a test and it takes about 10 seconds.
I want you to think about the last time you were in your parents room and I want you to count how many of these three
things happened.
One, they ate more in one sitting than they had eaten in a week, not a little more.
A plate, a plate with a second helping, maybe.
Two, they were awake and clear after days of sleeping through the afternoon.
They tracked the conversation.
They asked a question about somebody else's life.
Three, they asked for something specific, a food from a particular place, a person by name, a song, a shirt, something from 30 years ago that
they had no business remembering.
If two of those three happened, that was a rally.
And if it happened in the last week or two, then you are in the window I'm going to talk about for the rest of this
video.
And I want you to listen with a pencil in your hand.
If it hasn't happened yet and your mother or your father is in that slow part where the eating is going down and the sleeping is
going up, then it may still come.
And when it comes, I don't want you to be the family that spends it on hold with the pharmacy.
Let me tell you what happens in the kitchen, because that is where the rally does its damage.
When walls sat up that morning, do you know what happened in the next hour?
The phone tree.
Lorraine called her daughter in Houston and her daughter called her brother in Kerrville and her brother called his wife's sister.
And by noon, there were people on the road from three directions.
And every single one of them drove to Bandera believing the same thing.
He's better.
And around four o'clock, somebody, I'm not going to say who, because it doesn't matter, somebody said the sentence.
Maybe we should call the agency and see about stopping the hospice.
Because if he's eating, maybe he doesn't need it anymore.
Maybe we can save the money.
Maybe we can get him back to his own room instead of that hospital bed.
I have heard that sentence in about 200 kitchens.
And I want to tell you something about it.
And I want you to hear it the way I mean it.
The rally is not a reason to stop hospice.
The rally is the reason hospice exists.
you are not paying for a dying service honey you are paying or medicare is paying which is a different conversation i'm going to get to
for somebody to be with you in the week when the body does this the woman from hospice who comes on thursday and takes one look
at your father and says this is the rally this is expected here is what friday and saturday will look like that is what you're paying
for.
If you cancel on Tuesday because he ate eggs, then on Friday night at 11 o'clock when the breathing changes and nobody in that house knows
what they're looking at, you will be calling 911 and 911 will take him to a hospital and he will die in a hallway under fluorescent
lights with a stranger holding his hand.
I have seen that many times.
It is the thing that families carry for the rest of their lives.
So the first thing, the concrete thing, and this one costs nothing.
When the The rally comes, you call your hospice team that same day, and you say exactly these words.
My father had a very good day today.
He ate, he sat up, he was clear.
Is this what you call the rally?
Use that word, rally.
Every hospice team in this country knows that word.
And then ask the question that matters.
What should we expect tomorrow, and who do we call at 2 in the morning?
Write those two sentences down.
Seriously, put them in your phone right now before I say anything else, because when the day comes, and it will come, you will not be
able to think of them.
Now let me tell you about the second kind of rally, because this one nobody warns you about.
Senora Ines Garza had dementia, she was 86 and she lived off Bandera Road with her daughter Yolanda, and she had not said a full sentence
to anybody in about two years.
Two years.
She knew her daughter by the feel of her hands.
That was all.
She would look at Yolanda sometimes, with a face that was almost there, and then it would go away again.
In the fall of 2016, on a Thursday, Inés sat up in the bed and asked Yolanda for a cup of coffee from the HEB on
Bandera Road.
not coffee, coffee from the HEV, the one with the bakery where they used to go on Saturday mornings when Yolanda was a girl.
And she called Yolanda by her name.
She said, Yolanda, mija, I want a coffee.
Yolanda drove to the HEV.
She called me from the parking lot crying with the engine running.
She said, Rosa, she knows me.
She knew me.
She's in there.
And I said, Yolanda, I know, and I know what you're going to ask me.
And the answer is no, honey.
This is not the medicine working.
This is the rally.
And she said, I don't care what it is.
I'm getting her the coffee.
And she did.
And Ines drank about a third of it.
And she held Yolanda's hand.
And she said, thank you, mija.
And then she went back to sleep.
She died on Saturday morning while Yolanda was at that same HEB buying coffee for the second time.
Yolanda was not in the room.
I have thought about that for nine years.
Now, I want to be very careful here because I am not going to tell you that Yolanda did something wrong.
She didn't.
She went to get her mother coffee from the one place that meant something to that woman.
That was an act of love and I will not put a stone on it, but I will tell you what happened because it happens in
houses all over this city and I want you to be able to choose.
What happens is this.
The rally gives the family one small errand, one, and in that errand the dying person sometimes goes.
So here is the second concrete thing and it costs nothing either.
During the rally somebody stays in the room, not in the house, in the room.
If your mother sends you for coffee, you send somebody else, or you call the neighbor, or you call me, or you call the agency and
ask for the aid to come an hour early.
But somebody stays, and if nobody can stay, if you're alone, if it's three in the morning and you are the only person in that house,
then you don't leave.
You make the coffee from the pot on the counter and you tell her it's from the HEB.
She will not know and you will not have to carry that parking lot for the rest of your life.
That is not a lie, honey.
That is a kindness and I have done it.
Now let me tell you why this happens.
And here I have to be careful because this is the part where a chaplain can sound like she knows more than she does.
I don't know why it happens.
Nobody I ever sat with knew why it happened.
What I can tell you is what the medical team told me over and over in the car on the way back from a visit and
what I watched with my own two eyes for 34 years.
What they told me is that the body at the very end is not a machine running out of gas.
It is more like a house at night turning off the lights one room at a time and every so often in some houses one of
those lights comes back on for a couple of hours.
Not because the house is fixed, because something in there got one more moment.
The medical team had a name for the brain doing that.
Terminal lucidity.
That's the phrase you'll find if you go looking.
And it's a real phrase and there are researchers who study it and argue about it.
I'm not going to argue with any of them.
I'll tell you what I saw.
I saw people who had not spoken a word in weeks sit up and say something that made the whole room go quiet.
I saw a man who had not recognized his own son called him by his childhood nickname.
I saw Mrs.
Ophelia Washington, who sang in a Baptist church choir on the east side for 40 years and had not sung in a month, hummed through an
entire hymn on a Wednesday afternoon and die on the Thursday.
And I will tell you what I believe as a chaplain in my own words, and you can take it or leave it at this table.
I believe the rally is a conversation.
The person is not doing it for you.
The person is doing it for themselves and they are letting you watch because they know you need to see it.
It's the last thing they get to give you.
And what they're giving you is not a recovery.
It's a picture, a picture of them the way they want to be remembered, not the way they were on Tuesday with the sheet up to
the chin and the mouth open, the way they were at the table with the coffee laughing at something you said.
Every family I ever sat with that had a good rally and used it, remember their parent like that.
And every family that had a rally and spent it arguing about the will, remember the arguing.
That's not a coincidence, honey.
That's the whole thing.
So what do you do with the picture?
That's the next part.
And this is the part I want you to stay for.
I want you to do three things.
And the third one is the one nobody does.
The first one, you ask the questions you have been avoiding.
Not the big one.
Not are you scared?
That question puts a wall up.
Ask the small ones.
Ask her what her mother's kitchen smelled like.
Ask him who his best friend was when he was 12.
Ask her what she would have done differently if she had it to do over.
Ask them what they want you to know, not what they want you to have, what they want you to know.
I sat with a man in Leon Valley in 2009 who had not spoken to his brother in 19 years, 19 years over a truck, and
on the day of his rally he asked his wife to call his brother.
the brother came and the two of them sat in that room and did not say one word about the truck.
They talked about a dog they had when they were boys and they both cried and the brother told me at the funeral that was the
best afternoon of my life.
19 years honey and it took one Tuesday.
The second thing, you write it down or you record it.
Not for the internet, for you.
Put your phone on the table, face down, and press record, and let it run.
Because in about two weeks, you will not remember her voice.
I'm not being dramatic.
You will not remember the sound of it.
You'll remember the words, and you'll remember the face, and the voice will go, and a 20-minute recording of your mother talking about her mother's kitchen
is worth more than everything in that house.
And the third thing and this is the one that nobody does and it's the one that matters most.
You say the five sentences.
I learned them from Lola Benavides, the old chaplain who trained me in 1991.
She carried a rosary in her pocket and she was not delicate about anything and she told me the dying are never in a hurry Rosa,
we are and she said when the moment comes there are five sentences and you don't have to be a poet and you don't have to
be a priest and you don't have to be ready.
You just have to say them.
I forgive you.
Forgive me.
Thank you.
I love you.
Goodbye.
Five.
That's it.
Not five paragraphs.
Five sentences.
And I have watched grown men who could not say one of those to their own father.
And I have watched them say it in the last week.
And I have never once, not once, in 34 years seen a family regret saying one of those five things.
I have seen a great many families regret not saying them.
And here is the thing about the rally that nobody tells you.
The rally is the best chance you will ever get because on Tuesday when your father is sitting up and eating eggs and he's clear and
he's himself, you can say all five of those things and he will understand every word.
On Friday when he's back in the bed and the breathing has changed and he's not tracking, you can say them and I believe he hears
you.
I truly do.
But you will not know and not knowing is what keeps people up at night for years.
Say them on Tuesday.
Say them while he can answer.
Now, I want to talk to the family that is in the middle of this right now because I know you're watching this at 2 in
the morning with the phone on silent and I know exactly what your kitchen looks like because I have stood in about 300 of them.
Here's what's going to happen after the rally and I'm telling you so that when it happens you don't think something has gone wrong.
The rally ends usually within 24 to 48 hours.
Sometimes it fades out slowly over an afternoon.
Sometimes your father goes to sleep on Tuesday night after the best day he's had in a month and on Wednesday morning he does not wake
up the same.
He's quieter.
He's more tired than he was before the rally.
He may sleep for most of the day.
He may not want food again and this time he really doesn't want it and the house will do one of two things.
It will either panic or it will go very quiet.
The panic looks like this.
Somebody says we have to get him to the hospital.
Somebody says he's not eating, we have to do something.
Somebody calls the medical office and leaves a message and then calls again.
Somebody starts googling at the kitchen table at midnight and I understand every bit of it.
But I want to tell you what the hospice team is going to tell you when you call them and I want you to hear it
from me first so it doesn't feel like the door closing.
She's going to tell you that this is the way it goes.
The rally is the last thing the body had in the tank.
And after it, the body rests.
And then the body finishes.
She's going to tell you that the not eating is not the problem.
The not eating is part of it.
And forcing food at this stage can make your father uncomfortable.
She's going to tell you what to do about the dry mouth, the little sponge on a stick, the lip balm, the ice chip, and she
is going to tell you who to call at 2 in the morning.
And I want you to write that number on a piece of paper and tape it to the refrigerator because your phone will be dead and
your hands will be shaking and you will not be able to find it in the contacts.
And I want to say one more thing about this, and I'll say it carefully.
If your parent is on hospice and there are medicines in that house for comfort and the rally happens and somebody in the family says, Well,
he's better.
Let's keep it today.
You call your hospice team before you change anything.
Not me, not your cousin who used to work at a pharmacy, not the internet.
You call the hospice team and you ask what to do and you do what they say.
That is not a small thing.
I have seen families do it the other way and I'm not going to describe what happened because it isn't necessary.
So the third concrete thing, and this one does have a price, and I want to give it to you straight.
The rally is the moment to have the papers in order, not after, during.
I'm talking about a folder, a binder, a shoebox, I don't care what it is, with the things that somebody is going to need in the
next two weeks.
The will, or where the will is, the deed to the house, the car title, the bank and the name of the person at the bank,
the life insurance policy number and the phone number for the company, his social security number, her date of birth and her mother's maiden name, the
funeral home and whether he wanted to be buried or cremated and where.
And if you don't know where any of that is, then on Tuesday, while he is sitting up and clear, you ask him.
You ask him where the wheel is.
You ask him which funeral home.
You ask him if he wants the rosary or the hymn.
I have watched a woman in her 60s sit at a kitchen table for three hours with her dying father and a legal pad and get
all of it and she told me afterward it was the most useful three hours of her life.
Why does it matter so much?
Because of the money, honey.
Because the average funeral in this city runs somewhere between $7,000 and $12,000.
And the plot is often separate.
And the family that has not talked about it will spend the week after the death making decisions with a checkbook in one hand and a
grief counselor on the phone.
And the family that talked about it on a Tuesday will spend that week holding each other.
You don't have to have money set aside, you just have to have the conversation.
There is a difference between a family that is broke and grieving, and a family that is broke, grieving, and also does not know which funeral
home to call.
Now I want to talk about the thing that makes me angry, and I'm going to say it plainly, because I'm 62 years old and I
have earned the right.
A lot of what I just described is already paid for, not by you, by Medicare.
The hospice benefit under Medicare Part A pays for the hospice team that comes to the house.
It pays for the aide who comes to help your father bathe and change.
It pays for the social worker.
It pays for the chaplain.
That was me, honey.
That was my salary.
And it did not cost that family $1.
It pays for the hospital bed and the wheelchair and the oxygen and the supply.
It pays for the medicines that are for the terminal diagnosis and for comfort and the copay on those is capped at about $5 per prescription.
It also pays for respite care.
Up to 5 days in a facility so that you can sleep or go to your own appointment or go to your daughter's wedding.
days with a copay of about 5%.
And I want you to hear that because I have sat with families where the daughter had not slept more than three hours in a row
in six weeks, and I said the word respite, and she looked at me like I had offered her a trip to Hawaii.
It's there.
It's in the benefit.
And it pays for bereavement support for the family for up to 13 months after the death.
13 months, not one phone call, 13 months of somebody you can talk to and it is part of the benefit that you already have.
Now that's the benefit as Medicare describes it.
If you want the exact words and the exact list and the sentences to use when you ask for each one, I put everything I learned
in 34 years into five books and it's called the last month's playbook.
Medicare's hospice benefit already pays for and the words to ask for it, what the last months look like and what to say.
The link is in the first line of the description.
But before you go anywhere, I want to give you the last part, because the last part is the part I actually want you to take
to bed with you tonight.
If you get something out of this, if you're the daughter in the kitchen at 2 in the morning and this made you feel a little
less alone.
Do me a favor and hit that subscribe button and leave me a comment telling me who you're taking care of.
I read every one of them at this table with my coffee on Sunday mornings.
I really do.
And I pray for you.
I'm not going to make a show of it, but I do.
Now, tonight, not next week, tonight.
Go find a piece of paper and a pen, a real one, not your phone.
There's something about the hand that makes it stay.
Write five lines on that paper.
One, the name of your parents' hospice team and the after hours number and put it on the refrigerator with tape.
Two, the words you're going to say to the hospice team when the rally comes.
My father had a very good day.
He ate, he sat up, he was clear.
Is this what you call the rally?
What should we expect tomorrow and who do we call at 2 in the morning.
The name of one person you can call at 2 in the morning who is not family.
Not to help, just to sit on the phone with you.
The five sentences written out.
I forgive you, forgive me, thank you, I love you, goodbye.
Write them down even if you think you'll remember them, because you won't and because seeing them on paper makes it easier to say them out
loud the first time and the first time is the one that's hard.
And five, where the will is, where the deed is, which funeral home.
If you don't know, write I don't know and put a star next to it and the next time you're in that room and your mother
is having a good hour, you ask her.
That's it.
That's the whole thing, five lines on a piece of paper, and you are more prepared than 90% of the families I sat with in 34
years.
And when the day comes, and I'm sorry, honey, but it comes for all of us, and your father sits up in that bed and asks
you for huevos rancheros, I want you to think of me sitting at this table, and I want you to know two things.
One, this is not the medicine.
This is not the prayers.
This is the last gift and it is not for him, it's for you.
And two, you are not going to get this perfect.
Nobody does.
I didn't get it perfect with my own mother in March of 2015 and I had 30 years of training and a whole hospice team and
I still stood in that kitchen and cried into the sink.
You are going to forget something.
You are going to say the wrong thing.
You are going to leave the room at the wrong moment, like Yolanda did, and you are going to carry it, and that is what it
is to love somebody who is dying.
It is not a test you pass, it's a room you sit in, so sit in it, say the five sentences while he can answer.
Eat the huevos rancheros with him, and let him tell the story about the horse, and laugh at the part that isn't funny, and hold his
hand when he goes quiet and then let him go, honey.
Let him go.
And don't you dare spend that Tuesday on the phone with the insurance company.
Now, next week, I'm going to sit right here and tell you about the morning after.
The first morning, the house is quiet.
And the three things you should not do in that first hour.
And the one phone call that most families make too late and shouldn't make at all.
If you're going to be in that place, I want you to be here for it.
And if you're not, if your mother or your father is still in the good years, still driving you crazy, still calling you three times on
a Sunday, then go call them, not text them, call them, and ask them what their mother's kitchen smelled like.
That's all I have for you tonight, mija.
Go with God and go gently and call your hospice team.
